The early life stages of the Common earthworm (Lumbricus terrestris) are profoundly influenced by thermal conditions prevailing in the soil. In laboratory incubation trials, embryonated eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] were observed to hatch after a developmental period of approximately 90.0 days [ab = approximately 90.0 days]. This duration is notably extended compared to incubation under warmer regimes, reflecting a temperature-dependent metabolic slowing typical of oligochaetes. Upon eclosion, the freshly emerged juveniles exhibit a remarkably small body mass; each neonate weighs roughly 0.7 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.7 grams] immediately after hatching. This modest initial investment in offspring mass, combined with the protracted incubation at cooler temperatures, suggests an adaptive strategy that balances yolk provisioning against extended developmental risk in temperate soils. The fertilised ova from which these individuals arise begin as minuscule yolky structures; each individual egg has an initial wet weight of just 0.061 grams [Ww0 = 0.061 grams], a value that underscores the substantial proportional mass gain achieved during the embryonic interval within the protective cocoon.

In contrast, when embryonic development proceeds under warmer soil conditions, the thermal acceleration of physiological processes is clearly evident. At a stable incubation temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the period required for egg hatching is considerably compressed, with eclosion occurring approximately 70.0 days [ab = approximately 70.0 days] after oviposition. This reduction of roughly twenty days relative to the cooler regime highlights the strong thermal sensitivity of early organogenesis and yolk absorption in this species. Following the chorion rupture and the commencement of the yolk-sac larva phase, the newly emerged individuals begin exogenous feeding almost immediately, transitioning from an endotrophic to an exotrophic state. The relatively low neonatal wet weight of 0.7 grams [Wwb = 0.7 grams] at this warmer temperature remains consistent across incubation conditions, suggesting that the initial mass at emergence is a fixed ontogenetic trait rather than a temperature-dependent variable. These findings align well with comparative data from other members of the Lumbricidae family.

The post-embryonic growth trajectory of Lumbricus terrestris proceeds through a distinct juvenile phase before the onset of reproductive capability. Under the favourable thermal conditions of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the interval between hatching and the attainment of puberty is a relatively brief period. Field and laboratory measurements indicate that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 73.0 days [tp = approximately 73.0 days], a value that places this species among the faster-maturing members of t at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]he Lumbricidae. During this pre-reproductive stage, the immature individuals accumulate somatic tissue rapidly. The wet weight at puberty, the body mass at which individuals first develop a functional clitellum and become capable of gamete production, is approximately 5.0 grams [Wwp = approximately 5.0 grams]. Achieving this critical mass requires a sustained period of feeding on organic detritus within the soil horizon. This developmental benchmark signals the transition from the sub-adult stage to the reproductively active adult phase.

As Lumbricus terrestris continues its growth beyond the pubertal milestone, individuals ultimately approach a characteristic asymptotic body size. The maximum or ultimate wet weight recorded for fully grown, reproductively active adults is approximately 12.87 grams [Wwi = approximately 12.87 grams]. This adult body mass represents a substantial increase from the 5.0 grams [Wwp = 5.0 grams] observed at the initiation of reproductive activity, indicating continued somatic expansion well after the clitellum has formed. In terms of linear dimensions, the corresponding ultimate total length for these large individuals is around 22.5 centimeters [Li = around 22.5 centimeters]. These values for body size are typical for the species in productive temperate soils, though considerable variation exists depending on local food availability and population density. The elongated form of the adult worm is an adaptation for burrowing through the soil matrix, facilitating the ingestion of organic matter and the translocation of mineral particles that contribute to soil turnover and aeration.

The complete lifespan of Lumbricus terrestris under controlled laboratory conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] has been documented to extend to approximately 2601.0 days [am = approximately 2601.0 days], which equates to roughly seven years. This substantial longevity is remarkable for a terrestrial invertebrate of its size and places it among the longer-lived oligochaete species, reflecting a slow pace of life characterized by sustained reproductive output over many seasons. Long-term studies of marked individuals in semi-natural enclosures have confirmed that reproductive senescence is not abrupt; rather, adults maintain the capacity for cocoon production for several years after reaching sexual maturity. The combination of a moderate wet weight at puberty of 5.0 grams [Wwp = 5.0 grams] and a prolonged adult phase suggests that the lifetime reproductive effort of this species is heavily weighted toward repeated breeding events. This life-history strategy is well suited to the stable but resource-patchy environment of the soil horizon, where consistent investment in reproduction across multiple seasons can buffer against unpredictable fluctuations in food supply.
